title: Lalita and the sugarcane bow
hookLine: the gods are losing, so they build a fire, and a goddess rises out of it
carry: desire isn't the enemy; it belongs inside dharma
tomorrow: a hymn with no story, only names. why would that work?
last: BRAHMANDA: THE WHOLE UNIVERSE IN ONE EGG.

lines: A GODDESS RISES FROM THE FIRE.
cards: It's the moment in every group project when someone types: okay, nothing is working. The gods are there. A demon named Bhanda has taken their worlds, and every plan has failed.
So they build a fire for a great sacrifice and start offering into it, and in the telling, when there's nothing left to give, they offer themselves. The flames climb.
Something climbs with them: a goddess, young and shining. And what she's holding is not what anyone expects a warrior to hold.

teach.b: She is Lalita, and this is the Lalitopakhyana, the account of Lalita. Hayagriva, the horse-headed form of Vishnu, tells it to the sage Agastya.
In her hands: a noose, an elephant goad, a bow made of sugarcane, and arrows made of flowers. To see why, look at the enemy.

In the telling, Bhanda is born from ashes, the ashes of Kama, the god of desire, after Shiva burns him with the fire of his third eye. So the demon is desire that was burned but not gone, desire gone sour.
And the goddess rides out armed with sweetness and blossoms, the very things desire reaches for. With an army of goddesses behind her, she meets Bhanda, and he falls. Then the surprise.
After the battle, at the gods' asking, Kama is given back his life. The story doesn't end with desire wiped out. It ends with desire returned to the world, in the goddess's hand.
That's a real Hindu teaching, told as a story.

teach.h: KAMA: ONE OF LIFE'S FOUR AIMS.
teach.b: Kama, desire, is one of the four aims of a human life, beside dharma, right living, artha, a livelihood, and moksha, freedom. It isn't the enemy.
It belongs inside dharma. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says, in paraphrase: I am the desire that does not go against dharma.
Devotees in the Shri Vidya tradition worship Lalita as the great goddess, and some readers hear the battle as one fought inside a person.

how: Devotees of the goddess Lalita, especially in the Shri Vidya tradition, read and retell the Lalitopakhyana, and her hymn of names, which tradition places in the same Purana, is recited in homes and temples.

games.q: a friend says her goal this year is to want nothing at all. by the end of Lalita's story, what's closest to what it shows?
o: wanting isn't wiped out; kama is one of life's aims, held inside dharma.
wanting is the enemy; burn it to ash and you're free.
wanting is harmless, so it never needs steering.
games.why: desire burned to ash came back sour, as Bhanda. after Lalita's battle, Kama is given back his life. Hindu teaching counts kama among the four aims of life, inside dharma.

practice: If a candle or lamp is near, let your eyes rest on its flame; if not, any small light will do. Keep looking for the whole sit.
When a want comes up, don't push it away and don't chase it: set it beside the light, and go back to looking. If you pray, you can offer it there.
